claim: Ambra1 is a WD40 domain-containing protein involved in the development of the central nervous system, adult neurogenesis and vertebrate embryogenesis.
source: Ambra1 (activating molecule in Beclin1-regulated autophagy) is a WD40 domain-containing protein that is involved in the development of the central nervous system, adult neurogenesis and vertebrate embryogenesis (Benato et al., 2013; Fimia et al., 2007; Yazdankhah et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Benato et al., 2013; Fimia et al., 2007; Yazdankhah et al., 2014).

claim: Ambra1 is an autophagy regulator that binds to Beclin1 and plays a role in the initiation of autophagy required for neurogenesis.
source: It is an autophagy regulator, binding to Beclin1 and playing a role in the initiation of autophagy, which is required for neurogenesis (Fimia et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Fimia et al., 2007).

claim: When autophagy is not initiated, the Ambra1-Beclin1-Vps34 complex is bound to the dynein motor complex.
source: When autophagy is not initiated, the Ambra1-Beclin1-Vps34 complex is bound to the dynein motor complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about Ambra1 function in autophagy regulation.

claim: Upon induction of autophagy, Ambra1 gets phosphorylated by the kinase ULK1, resulting in its release from the dynein complex.
source: Upon induction of autophagy, Ambra1 gets phosphorylated by the kinase ULK1, resulting in its release from the dynein complex (Di Bartolomeo et al., 2010; Strappazzon et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Di Bartolomeo et al., 2010; Strappazzon et al., 2011).

claim: Ambra1 function is negatively regulated by mTOR phosphorylation, which suppresses its binding to the E3-ligase TRAF6 and ULK1 ubiquitylation, thus controlling ULK1 stability and function.
source: Ambra1 function is negatively regulated by mTOR phosphorylation, which suppresses its binding to the E3-ligase TRAF6 and ULK1 ubiquitylation, thus controlling ULK1 stability and function (Nazio et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Nazio et al., 2013).

claim: During apoptosis, Ambra1 expression is regulated by caspase-mediated cleavage as well as degradation by calpains.
source: During apoptosis, Ambra1 expression is regulated by caspase-mediated cleavage as well as degradation by calpains (Pagliarini et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Pagliarini et al., 2012).

claim: Ambra1 is ubiquitylated and subsequently degraded by RNF2.
source: a recent study reported the ubiquitylation and subsequent degradation of Ambra1 by RNF2 (Xia et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Xia et al., 2014).

claim: Ambra1 supports the binding of c-Myc to the phosphatase PP2A, leading ultimately to c-Myc degradation and reduced cell proliferation and tumourigenesis.
source: Further, Ambra1 has been reported to support the binding of c-Myc to the phosphatase PP2A, leading ultimately to c-Myc degradation and reduced cell proliferation and tumourigenesis (Cianfanelli et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Cianfanelli et al., 2015).

claim: Ambra1 overexpression in cholangiocarcinoma has been correlated with invasion and poor survival.
source: whilst a different study implied that Ambra1 overexpression in cholangiocarcinoma has been correlated with invasion and poor survival (Nitta et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Nitta et al., 2014).

claim: Ambra1 is a focal adhesion kinase (FAK)- and Src-binding partner.
source: In the present study, we found that Ambra1 is a focal adhesion kinase (FAK)- and Src-binding partner.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: FAK-dependent phenotypes include cancer cell polarisation and directional migration, depending primarily on FAK's protein scaffolding activities, including binding to actin regulators like Eps8, Arp3 and RACK1.
source: We have previously shown that FAK-dependent phenotypes include cancer cell polarisation and directional migration, depending primarily on FAK's protein scaffolding activities, including binding to actin regulators like Eps8, Arp3 and RACK1 (Schoenherr et al., 2014; Serrels et al., 2010, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research by the authors (Schoenherr et al., 2014; Serrels et al., 2010, 2007).

claim: Genetic depletion of FAK, or detachment of FAK-expressing cells, cause active Src to be trafficked from focal adhesions at the cell periphery to intracellular puncta containing autophagy proteins.
source: In particular, genetic depletion of FAK, or detachment of FAK-expressing cells, cause active Src to be trafficked from focal adhesions at the cell periphery to intracellular puncta containing autophagy proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript.

claim: Adhesion-stress-induced autophagy is FAK and adhesion dependent rather than nutrient dependent, in contrast to classical, starvation-induced autophagy.
source: We termed this 'adhesion-stress-induced autophagy', and it is FAK and adhesion dependent rather than nutrient dependent, in contrast to the classical, starvation-induced autophagy.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and inference from the authors' previous work.

claim: Adhesion-stress-induced autophagy provides a novel mechanism for coping with high levels of active Src and other oncogenic kinases like Ret, which are not spatially controlled in the usual way by their binding to FAK.
source: It provides a novel mechanism for coping with high levels of active Src, and other oncogenic kinases like Ret, which are not spatially controlled in the usual way by their binding to FAK (Sandilands et al., 2012a, 2012b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research (Sandilands et al., 2012a, 2012b).

claim: Ambra1 is critically involved in Src/FAK-dependent cancer cell polarisation and chemotactic invasion.
source: We found that Ambra1 is critically involved in Src/FAK-dependent cancer cell polarisation and chemotactic invasion.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from polarisation and invasion assays shown in the manuscript.

claim: In FAK-depleted SCC cells, Ambra1 controls the targeting of active Src to intracellular autophagic puncta.
source: In FAK-depleted SCC cells, Ambra1 controls the targeting of active Src to intracellular autophagic puncta.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence and knockdown experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: Ambra1-mediated control of active Src targeting is mediated by the novel Ambra1-binding proteins Dynactin 1 (Dctn1) and interferon-induced transmembrane protein 3 (IFITM3).
source: This is mediated by the novel Ambra1-binding proteins Dynactin 1 (Dctn1; also known as p150Glued) and interferon-induced transmembrane protein 3 (IFITM3), which together with Ambra1, are critical to trafficking processes that control spatial Src activity and Src-dependent phenotypes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry, co-immunoprecipitation, and knockdown experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: A FAK mutant that is not able to bind Ambra1 promotes increased cell adhesion and invasion by retaining more phospho-FAK (pFAK) and phospho-Src (pSrc) at focal adhesions.
source: A FAK mutant that is not able to bind Ambra1 promotes increased cell adhesion and invasion by retaining more phospho-FAK (pFAK) and phospho-Src (pSrc) at focal adhesions – showing that Ambra1 can both positively and negatively regulate the amount of active Src at cellular adhesion sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from adhesion assays, invasion assays, and immunofluorescence shown in the manuscript.

claim: Ambra1 can both positively and negatively regulate the amount of active Src at cellular adhesion sites.
source: A FAK mutant that is not able to bind Ambra1 promotes increased cell adhesion and invasion by retaining more phospho-FAK (pFAK) and phospho-Src (pSrc) at focal adhesions – showing that Ambra1 can both positively and negatively regulate the amount of active Src at cellular adhesion sites.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing different effects of Ambra1 depending on FAK status.

claim: Ambra1 and its key interacting partners Dynactin 1 and IFITM3 are at the heart of an intracellular trafficking network that acts as a 'spatial rheostat' for phospho-Src and Src/FAK-mediated cancer processes.
source: Overall, these data imply a novel role for the autophagic protein Ambra1, and its key interacting partners Dynactin 1 and IFITM3, at the heart of an intracellular trafficking network that, in turn, acts as a 'spatial rheostat' for phospho-Src and Src/FAK-mediated cancer processes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and inference from the collective results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ambra1 was discovered as a FAK binding partner in a phage display screen.
source: We discovered Ambra1 in a phage display screen for novel FAK binding partners.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental method described in the manuscript.

claim: Ambra1 co-immunoprecipitates with FAK in SCC cells.
source: First, we confirmed Ambra1 as a novel FAK binding partner in SCC cells by reciprocal co-immunoprecipitations (co-IPs; Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Ambra1 displays diffuse cytoplasmic localisation with some at focal adhesions in both SCC FAK-WT and FAK -/- cells.
source: In both SCC FAK-WT and FAK -/- cells, Ambra1 displayed diffuse cytoplasmic localisation with some at focal adhesions (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Ambra1 co-localises with FAK and Paxillin at isolated focal adhesions.
source: Therefore, we isolated focal adhesions from FAK-WT and FAK -/- cells by hydrodynamic force and found that Ambra1 co-localised with FAK and Paxillin at isolated focal adhesions (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from isolated focal adhesions shown in Figure 1E and supplementary figures.

claim: Ambra1 localises to hydrodynamic force-isolated nascent focal adhesions, marked by the presence of RACK1, in both FAK-WT and FAK -/- cells.
source: Additionally, Ambra1 localised to hydrodynamic force-isolated nascent focal adhesions, marked by the presence of RACK1 (de Hoog et al., 2004; Serrels et al., 2010, 2007), in both FAK-WT and FAK -/- cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1F and citations to previous research (de Hoog et al., 2004; Serrels et al., 2010, 2007).

claim: Ambra1 is present at focal adhesions at the cell-surface interface as shown by TIRF microscopy.
source: In addition, we found that Ambra1 was present at focal adhesions at the cell-surface interface by Total Internal Reflection Fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy; there was partial overlap with pSrc Y416 and FAK, suggesting that, as with other autophagy proteins we have reported previously (Sandilands et al., 2012a; Schoenherr et al., 2014), there are pools of Ambra1 discretely present at sub-locations within focal adhesions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G; Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in supplementary figures and citations to previous research (Sandilands et al., 2012a; Schoenherr et al., 2014).

claim: Ambra1 and Src, including active phospho-Src (pSrc; pY416), form a biochemical complex both in FAK-expressing and -deficient SCC cells.
source: Ambra1 and Src, including active phospho-Src (pSrc; pY416), formed a biochemical complex both in FAK-expressing and -deficient SCC cells as shown by co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Ambra1 localises to intracellular puncta that contain autophagy-regulating proteins like LC3B.
source: Using immunofluorescence, we found that Ambra1 localised to intracellular puncta that contain autophagy-regulating proteins like LC3B (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: In FAK-deficient SCC cells, Ambra1 co-localises with pSrc, indicating that active Src and Ambra1 localise to the same intracellular puncta.
source: In FAK-deficient SCC cells, Ambra1 co-localised with pSrc, indicating that active Src and Ambra1 localised to the same intracellular puncta, described previously to contain autophagy proteins (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Ambra1 co-immunoprecipitates with LC3B.
source: The localisation of Ambra1 in these autophagosomes was consistent with co-immunoprecipitation with LC3B, providing evidence that they were present in the same biochemical complex (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: There is a reduced steady state level of the lipidated form of LC3B (LC3B II) in SCC FAK -/- cells.
source: We note that there was a reduced steady state level of the lipidated form of LC3B (LC3B II) in the SCC FAK -/- cells (the significance of this is unknown; [Sandilands et al., 2012a]).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation and citation to previous research (Sandilands et al., 2012a).

claim: Knockdown of endogenous Ambra1 results in the redistribution of active Src from intracellular puncta back to focal adhesions in FAK -/- cells.
source: Knockdown of endogenous Ambra1 either by the pool of four siRNAs (Figure 2G,H) or two individual siRNAs (Figure 2I,J) resulted in the redistribution of active Src from intracellular puncta back to focal adhesions in FAK -/- cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdown and immunofluorescence shown in Figure 2G-J.

claim: Ambra1 is required for the trafficking of active Src from focal adhesions to intracellular autophagic puncta.
source: Taken together, these data imply that Ambra1 is required for the trafficking of active Src from focal adhesions to intracellular autophagic puncta.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing redistribution of active Src upon Ambra1 knockdown.

claim: Amongst the binding partners of Ambra1, pSrc Y416, and FAK are proteins involved in regulating intracellular trafficking.
source: Amongst the binding partners of all three 'baits' were proteins that are involved in regulating intracellular trafficking, raising the possibility that Ambra1 is part of a Src/FAK 'trafficking network' (Figure 3A; Supplementary file 1–3).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and network analysis shown in Figure 3A and supplementary files.

claim: The interaction between Ambra1 and Dynactin 1 appears to be enriched in FAK-deficient cells from proteomics analyses.
source: These were Dynactin 1, whose interaction with Ambra1 appeared to be enriched in FAK-deficient cells from proteomics analyses (Figure 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 3.

claim: IFITM3 is positioned at the centre of the trafficking network as it binds to all three of Ambra1, pSrc and FAK.
source: and IFITM3, which was positioned at the centre of the trafficking network as it bound to all three of Ambra1, pSrc and FAK (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomics data and network analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Dynactin 1 (Dctn1) is a component of the dynactin complex and is involved in dynein-mediated transport along microtubules, enhancing motor processivity.
source: Dctn1 (Dynactin 1) is a component of the dynactin complex and is involved in dynein-mediated transport along microtubules, enhancing motor processivity (Culver-Hanlon et al., 2006; King and Schroer, 2000; Waterman-Storer et al., 1995)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Culver-Hanlon et al., 2006; King and Schroer, 2000; Waterman-Storer et al., 1995).

claim: Dynactin 1 mediates trafficking and maturation of EGFR and lysosomes.
source: and mediating trafficking and maturation of EGFR and lysosomes (Kedashiro et al., 2015b; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Kedashiro et al., 2015b; Li et al., 2014).

claim: The interaction between Ambra1 and Dynactin 1 was confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation.
source: We confirmed the interaction between Ambra1 and Dynactin 1 by co-IP, thereby validating the interaction identified by mass spectrometry (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: IFITM3 blocks cellular entry of viruses.
source: IFITM3, which forms a central node linking the Ambra1, pSrc and FAK trafficking networks (Figure 3A), is known to block cellular entry of viruses (Amini-Bavil-Olyaee et al., 2013; Brass et al., 2009; Feeley et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2011; Lu et al., 2011; Weidner et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Amini-Bavil-Olyaee et al., 2013; Brass et al., 2009; Feeley et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2011; Lu et al., 2011; Weidner et al., 2010).

claim: IFITM3 traffics with Rab7 and LAMP1.
source: to traffic with Rab7 and LAMP1, and to interact with v-ATPase on endosomes to enable clathrin localisation (Feeley et al., 2011; Wee et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Feeley et al., 2011; Wee et al., 2012).

claim: IFITM3 interacts with v-ATPase on endosomes to enable clathrin localisation.
source: to traffic with Rab7 and LAMP1, and to interact with v-ATPase on endosomes to enable clathrin localisation (Feeley et al., 2011; Wee et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Feeley et al., 2011; Wee et al., 2012).

claim: IFITM3 is highly expressed in many cancers.
source: IFITM3 is highly expressed in many cancers (Andreu et al., 2006; Hu et al., 2014; Li et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Andreu et al., 2006; Hu et al., 2014; Li et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2013).

claim: IFITM3 has been implicated in tumour cell proliferation, migration and invasion.
source: and has been variously implicated in tumour cell proliferation, migration and invasion (Hu et al., 2014; Li et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Hu et al., 2014; Li et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2013).

claim: The interaction between Ambra1 and IFITM3 was confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation.
source: We confirmed the interaction between Ambra1 and IFITM3 (Figure 3C)
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The interaction between FAK and IFITM3 was confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation.
source: FAK and IFITM3 (Figure 3D)
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The interaction between pSrc and IFITM3 was confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation.
source: and pSrc and IFITM3 (Figure 3E) by co-IPs.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The interactions between IFITM3 and both Ambra1 and pSrc appear to be enriched in FAK-expressing cells due to increased IFITM3 expression levels, caused by FAK-dependent IFITM3 transcription.
source: The interactions between IFITM3 and both Ambra1 and pSrc appeared to be enriched in FAK-expressing cells due to increased IFITM3 expression levels, caused by FAK-dependent IFITM3 transcription (not shown; (Figure 3A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation and inference from the data.

claim: IFITM3 is present at focal adhesions, as shown by immunoblotting of isolated focal adhesion preparations.
source: and we believe that IFITM3 is present at focal adhesions, shown by immunoblotting of isolated focal adhesion preparations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Knockdown of IFITM3 does not affect the Ambra1-pSrc interaction.
source: While knockdown of IFITM3 did not affect the Ambra1-pSrc interaction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C)
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data after IFITM3 knockdown shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: IFITM3 depletion reduces the interaction between FAK and active pSrc.
source: IFITM3 depletion reduced the interaction between FAK and active pSrc, indicating that IFITM3 is involved in the optimal association of Src to FAK (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E)
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data after IFITM3 knockdown shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: IFITM3 is involved in the optimal association of Src to FAK, likely through regulating their precise localisation.
source: IFITM3 depletion reduced the interaction between FAK and active pSrc, indicating that IFITM3 is involved in the optimal association of Src to FAK (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E), likely through regulating their precise localisation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and inference from the results.

claim: IFITM3 is a central component of a trafficking network linking Ambra1, FAK and active Src.
source: Thus, interaction network analysis coupled with co-immunoprecipitations suggest that IFITM3 is a central component of a trafficking network linking Ambra1, FAK and active Src (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by network analysis and co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Suppression of Dynactin 1 expression by siRNA results in significant redistribution of active pSrc from intracellular autophagic puncta to focal adhesions in FAK-deficient SCC cells.
source: We transiently knocked down endogenous Dynactin 1 (Figure 4A) or IFITM3 (Figure 4D) by siRNA, and analysed the localisation of active pSrc in FAK-deficient SCC cells. In both cases, suppression of protein expression resulted in significant redistribution of active pSrc from intracellular autophagic puncta to focal adhesions (Figure 4B,C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Figure 4E,F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B respectively)
evidence: The claim is supported by siRNA knockdown and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A-C and supplementary figures.

claim: Suppression of IFITM3 expression by siRNA results in significant redistribution of active pSrc from intracellular autophagic puncta to focal adhesions in FAK-deficient SCC cells.
source: We transiently knocked down endogenous Dynactin 1 (Figure 4A) or IFITM3 (Figure 4D) by siRNA, and analysed the localisation of active pSrc in FAK-deficient SCC cells. In both cases, suppression of protein expression resulted in significant redistribution of active pSrc from intracellular autophagic puncta to focal adhesions (Figure 4B,C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Figure 4E,F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B respectively)
evidence: The claim is supported by siRNA knockdown and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D-F and supplementary figures.

claim: In FAK-expressing cells, knockdown of Dynactin 1 or IFITM3 has no visible effect on active pSrc distribution.
source: while in FAK-expressing cells, knockdown of Dynactin 1 or IFITM3 had no visible effect on their distribution.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation from immunofluorescence data.

claim: Ambra1 is part of a functional trafficking network that precisely regulates the spatial distribution of Src activity.
source: These data imply that Ambra1 is part of a functional trafficking network that precisely regulates the spatial distribution of Src activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the collective experimental data on Ambra1, Dynactin 1, and IFITM3.

claim: Ambra1 functions via interaction with proteins involved in intracellular trafficking, including Dynactin 1 and IFITM3.
source: Mechanistically, Ambra1 functions via interaction with proteins involved in intracellular trafficking, including Dynactin 1 and IFITM3; the latter lies at the centre of linked Ambra1, pSrc, and FAK interactomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing interactions and functional effects.

claim: Knockdown of Ambra1 results in significant loss of polarisation towards a monolayer wound in FAK-expressing SCC cells.
source: We therefore knocked down Ambra1, and found that there was significant loss of polarisation towards a monolayer wound in FAK-expressing SCC cells, as judged by the direction of the Golgi apparatus (stained with GM130).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from polarisation assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: In FAK-deficient cells, knockdown of Ambra1 has no further effect on the already suppressed polarisation of cells towards a wound.
source: This was in contrast to FAK-deficient cells, in which knockdown of Ambra1 had no further effect on the already suppressed polarisation of cells towards a wound (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from polarisation assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The role of Ambra1 in polarisation was confirmed using Ambra1 +/+ and -/- MEFs.
source: The role of Ambra1 in polarisation was confirmed using Ambra1 +/+ and -/- MEFs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from polarisation assays using MEFs shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Ambra1 is required for chemotactic invasion into growth factor-reduced Matrigel in FAK-expressing cells.
source: In addition, we found that Ambra1 was required for chemotactic invasion into growth factor-reduced Matrigel in FAK-expressing cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from invasion assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: In FAK-deficient cells, Ambra1 knockdown has no effect on invasion, which is already suppressed.
source: whilst there was no effect in FAK-deficient cells, which, as we described previously, do not invade into Matrigel (Serrels et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citation to previous research (Serrels et al., 2012).

claim: Ambra1 has a previously unknown role in cancer cell polarisation and invasion that is Src/FAK dependent.
source: These results describe a previously unknown role for Ambra1 in cancer cell polarisation and invasion that is Src/FAK dependent.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data on polarisation and invasion assays.

claim: The Ambra1 binding site in FAK was mapped to amino acids P875 and P881.
source: The Ambra1 binding site in FAK was mapped by peptide array binding analysis as described previously (Schoenherr et al., 2014; Serrels et al., 2007), which resulted in identification of two amino acids in FAK that were required for optimal direct binding of Ambra1, i.e. amino acids P875 and P881.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from peptide array binding analysis and citations to previous methods (Schoenherr et al., 2014; Serrels et al., 2007).

claim: The FAK P875A/P881A (AA) mutant causes reduced binding of Ambra1 to FAK within cells.
source: These prolines (P) were mutated to alanines (A), and the resulting FAK P875A/P881A (AA) mutant caused reduced binding of Ambra1 to FAK within cells (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: The interaction between FAK and p130Cas is more modestly affected by the P875A/P881A mutation compared to the Ambra1-FAK interaction.
source: The interaction between FAK and p130Cas, which also binds FAK at a similar proline-rich region but not the same combination of amino acids (P715, P718, P878 and P881; ref. [Harte et al., 1996]), was more modestly affected by the P875A/P881A mutation (quantified in Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5A-C and citation to previous research (Harte et al., 1996).

claim: After 20 and 60 min, FAK P875A/P881A and FAK -/- cells attach to fibronectin-coated dishes to a higher degree than FAK-WT cells.
source: We found that after 20 and 60 min, FAK P875A/P881A and FAK -/- cells attached to a higher degree than FAK-WT cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from adhesion assays shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In already adhered FAK P875A/P881A cells, there is more intense pSrc staining at focal adhesions compared to FAK-WT cells.
source: Furthermore, in already adhered FAK P875A/P881A cells (Figure 5E, middle panels), we found that there was more intense pSrc staining at focal adhesions when compared to FAK-WT cells (Figure 5E, top panels)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In FAK -/- cells, pSrc is present at intracellular autophagic puncta.
source: or FAK -/- cells, in which pSrc was present at intracellular autophagic puncta (Figure 5E, lower panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: There are no significant changes in the number or size of focal adhesions in FAK P875A/P881A cells compared to FAK-WT cells.
source: While there was more intense staining of active pSrc at focal adhesions in FAK P857A/P881A cells, there were no significant changes in the number or size of focal adhesions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The increased staining of pSrc and pFAK Y397 in FAK P875A/P881A cells was confirmed by immunoblotting isolated focal adhesion preparations.
source: The increased staining of pSrc (and pFAK Y397; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) in FAK P875A/P881A cells was confirmed by immunoblotting isolated focal adhesion preparations (Figure 5G, right panels, red dots; quantified as phospho/total Src (and phospho/total FAK) in Figure 5H)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data from isolated focal adhesions shown in Figure 5G,H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Both active pSrc and pFAK are elevated relative to total Src and FAK, respectively, in FAK P875A/P881A cells.
source: demonstrating that both active pSrc and pFAK were elevated relative to total Src and FAK, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: pPaxillin Y118 is elevated in FAK P875A/P881A cells, reflecting specific retention of phospho- and activated- focal adhesion components at focal adhesions when FAK cannot bind to Ambra1.
source: This was true also of pPaxillin Y118 (Figure 5G, right panels), reflecting specific retention of phospho- and activated- focal adhesion components at focal adhesions when FAK cannot bind to Ambra1.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The FAK–Ambra1 complex is crucial to orchestrate the selective removal of active focal adhesion components from focal adhesions or to promote their turnover at these adhesion sites.
source: This implies that the FAK–Ambra1 complex is crucial to orchestrate the selective removal of active focal adhesion components from focal adhesions or to promote their turnover at these adhesion sites.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing elevated phospho-proteins when FAK cannot bind Ambra1.

claim: The elevated levels of active components retained at focal adhesions when the binding of FAK to Ambra1 is impaired may contribute to the enhanced adhesion at early times after plating on extracellular matrix.
source: The elevated levels of active components retained at focal adhesions when the binding of FAK to Ambra1 is impaired may contribute to the enhanced adhesion at early times after plating on extracellular matrix (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Elevated active pSrc and pFAK at focal adhesions in FAK P875A/P881A cells is associated with enhanced invasive migration.
source: We found that elevated active pSrc and pFAK at focal adhesions in FAK P875A/P881A cells was associated with enhanced invasive migration (Figure 6A,B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from invasion assays shown in Figure 6A,B.
